## What This Pattern Is For

Use the Get Unstuck pattern when you've hit a wall — something isn't working, you don't know why, and you're not sure what to try next. This pattern is for diagnosing problems and finding a path forward, not just getting a fix handed to you.

Good examples of when to Get Unstuck:
- Your code runs but produces the wrong output and you can't figure out why
- You get an error message you don't understand
- Something worked yesterday and stopped working today
- You know *what* you want to do but can't figure out *how* to approach it
- You've tried multiple fixes and none of them worked
- Your argument or writing isn't coming together and you don't know why

## Ask for Explanations, Not Just Fixes

When you're stuck, the tempting move is to ask the AI to just fix the problem. That works in the short term — but you'll hit the same wall again, and you still won't know how to get past it.

The Get Unstuck pattern is more valuable when you ask the AI to help you *understand* what's wrong, not just hand you a corrected version.

**Just a fix:**
> "Fix my conclusion paragraph."

You get a rewritten conclusion. It might sound better, but you have no idea what was actually wrong with yours or how to write a stronger one next time.

**Understanding the problem:**
> "My conclusion feels weak but I can't figure out why. Can you explain what a conclusion needs to do, identify what mine is missing, and walk me through what changes would fix it — and why?"

Now you understand what went wrong. Next time you'll recognize it faster.

The same principle applies to code:

**Just a fix:**
> "Fix this function."

**Understanding the problem:**
> "My Python function is returning the wrong value. Can you look at my logic, explain where it's going wrong and why, and then walk me through what a fix would look like?"

## Share Only the Relevant Context

When you're stuck, you might be tempted to paste in your entire project and ask the AI to figure it out. Resist that. A focused, well-scoped prompt gets a much more useful response than dumping everything in and hoping for the best.

Share what's directly relevant to the problem:
- The specific section, function, or passage that isn't working
- The error message, exactly as it appears
- What you expected to happen vs. what actually happened
- What you've already tried

**Too broad:**
> "Something is wrong with my essay. Can you find it?"

**Well-scoped:**
> "My second body paragraph feels disconnected from my thesis. Here's my thesis and the paragraph in question. I think the issue might be that my evidence doesn't clearly link back to my main argument — but I'm not sure."

The same applies to code:

**Too broad:**
> "Here's all my code. Something is broken. Can you find it?"

**Well-scoped:**
> "My `calculate_average()` function is returning 0 instead of the correct value. Here's the function and a sample input. I already confirmed the input isn't empty — the problem seems to be in the math."

## You Stay in Control of the Decisions

The AI can suggest a direction. It can explain why something is broken. It can propose a fix. But *you* decide what to actually do.

This matters because:
- The AI's suggested fix might work for the immediate problem but introduce a new one elsewhere
- The AI doesn't know your full project, your constraints, or your goals
- The "correct" solution might not be the right choice for your specific situation

After you get a response, ask yourself: *Does this make sense for my situation? Are there any tradeoffs or side effects I should think about?* Don't just apply the suggestion — understand it first.

## Example Prompts

**Diagnosing a logic bug:**
> "My Python function is supposed to go through a list of test scores and count how many are above 80, but it's always returning 0. Here's the function. Can you explain what the logic error is and why it's producing the wrong result, then walk me through what a fix would look like?"

**Something on a web page isn't working:**
> "I added a button to my HTML page that's supposed to show a hidden message when clicked, but nothing happens when I click it. I've checked that the button exists in the HTML. Can you look at my HTML and JavaScript and explain why the click isn't triggering anything, and walk me through what I'd need to change?"

**Stuck at the start — not sure how to approach something:**
> "I need to write a Python script that reads a text file and counts how many times each word appears, then prints the top 10 most common words. I know what I want it to do but I don't know where to start. Can you walk me through a few different ways I could approach this — not full code, just the logic — so I can pick one and build it myself?"

**Stuck on writing, not code:**
> "I'm trying to write the conclusion for my history essay comparing the causes of World War I and World War II, but every version I write feels like it's just restating the introduction. Can you look at my intro and the draft conclusion I have and explain what's going wrong? What does a conclusion need to do that mine isn't doing?"

**When previous fixes haven't worked:**
> "I've been trying to fix a bug where my game character doesn't stop moving when it hits the edge of the screen. I've tried adding a boundary check inside the movement function (it's there), and I added a print statement to confirm it's being reached (it is). But the character still goes off screen. Here's the relevant code. What else could be causing this, and what would you check next?"

## What to Do After You Get Unstuck

- **Understand the explanation** before you apply any fix — if you can't follow the reasoning, ask for a clearer walkthrough
- **Test the fix** and check that it actually solves the problem without breaking something else
- **Note what you learned** — what was the underlying pattern? Where else in your project might the same issue exist?
- **Don't treat it as done** just because the immediate problem is gone — make sure you understand why the fix worked

Getting unstuck isn't the finish line. Understanding what got you stuck — and why the fix works — is what makes you stronger next time.
